title: Pure Functions
explanation: A pure function always produces the same output for the same input and has no side effects. It doesn't modify external state, read from external sources, or depend on anything other than its arguments.
analogy: Like a mathematical formula: f(x) = x + 2 always gives the same answer for the same x. It doesn't check the weather or change your bank balance while calculating.
tiny_visual_key: same input arrows pointing to same output box, no external arrows
example: Pure: add(a, b) => a + b. Impure: getTime() returns different values, or a function that modifies a global counter.
why_it_matters: Pure functions are predictable, testable, and cacheable. They eliminate entire categories of bugs related to shared state and make code easier to reason about and parallelize.
checkpoint_question: Why can pure functions be safely cached (memoized)?
expected_answer: Because they always return the same output for the same input, the result can be stored and reused without recomputation, knowing it will always be correct.
common_mistake: Thinking a function is pure because it looks simple, but it reads from a database or uses Math.random() internally.
key_insight: Purity is about referential transparency - you can replace a function call with its result without changing program behavior.

title: Immutability
explanation: Immutable data cannot be changed after creation. Instead of modifying existing data, you create new data with the desired changes. The original remains unchanged.
analogy: Like a printed photograph. You can't change it, but you can make a copy with modifications (crop, filter). The original photo stays the same forever.
tiny_visual_key: locked box with arrow to new modified box, original unchanged
example: Instead of arr.push(4), use [...arr, 4]. Instead of obj.name = 'new', use {...obj, name: 'new'}.
why_it_matters: Immutability eliminates bugs from unexpected mutations, makes change tracking trivial, enables safe sharing across threads, and simplifies undo/redo functionality.
checkpoint_question: How does immutability help with debugging state changes?
expected_answer: Since data can't change, you can keep references to all previous states. When something goes wrong, you can inspect any historical state and see exactly when/where new state was created.
common_mistake: Thinking immutability means never changing anything - it means creating new values rather than mutating existing ones.
key_insight: Persistent data structures use structural sharing to make immutable updates efficient - they share unchanged parts with the original.

title: First-Class Functions
explanation: Functions are first-class citizens when they can be treated like any other value: assigned to variables, passed as arguments, returned from other functions, and stored in data structures.
analogy: Like treating recipes as ingredients themselves. You can put a recipe in a cookbook, hand it to someone, get a recipe back as a gift, or combine recipes to make new ones.
tiny_visual_key: function box being passed around like regular data boxes
example: const greet = name => 'Hello ' + name; const funcs = [greet, console.log]; funcs[0]('World');
why_it_matters: First-class functions enable higher-order functions, callbacks, and functional composition - the building blocks of functional programming.
checkpoint_question: What can you do with first-class functions that you couldn't with regular functions?
expected_answer: Pass them as arguments to other functions, return them from functions, store them in arrays/objects, and assign them to variables for later use.
common_mistake: Confusing function references (fn) with function calls (fn()). Passing fn passes the function itself; passing fn() passes its return value.
key_insight: First-class functions are what make functional programming possible - without them, higher-order patterns couldn't exist.

title: Higher-Order Functions
explanation: A higher-order function either takes one or more functions as arguments, returns a function, or both. They abstract over actions, not just values.
analogy: Like a chef instructor who doesn't just cook, but teaches cooking techniques. They take in a student (function) and return an improved chef (enhanced function).
tiny_visual_key: big function box containing smaller function boxes
example: map, filter, reduce are higher-order because they take a function argument. A function factory that returns functions is also higher-order.
why_it_matters: Higher-order functions enable powerful abstractions like mapping, filtering, and composing. They let you build complex behavior from simple, reusable pieces.
checkpoint_question: Why is Array.map considered a higher-order function?
expected_answer: Because it takes a function as an argument (the transformation to apply to each element) and uses that function internally to process the array.
common_mistake: Writing loops when map/filter/reduce would be clearer. Higher-order functions express intent better than manual iteration.
key_insight: Higher-order functions let you parameterize behavior, not just data - making code more flexible and reusable.

title: Closures
explanation: A closure is a function that remembers and accesses variables from its outer scope even after the outer function has finished executing. The inner function 'closes over' those variables.
analogy: Like a backpack you pack before leaving home. Even when you're far away, you still have access to what you packed. The function carries its environment with it.
tiny_visual_key: inner function bubble connected to outer scope variables
example: function makeCounter() { let count = 0; return () => ++count; } The returned function remembers 'count' even after makeCounter returns.
why_it_matters: Closures enable data privacy, stateful functions without classes, partial application, and are fundamental to how callbacks and event handlers work.
checkpoint_question: How can closures be used to create private variables?
expected_answer: Variables in the outer function's scope are only accessible through the returned inner function. There's no other way to access or modify them, creating true privacy.
common_mistake: Not realizing closures capture variable references, not values. In a loop, all closures may share the same variable unless you create new scope.
key_insight: Closures are how JavaScript implements encapsulation without classes - they provide true private state.

title: Currying
explanation: Currying transforms a function that takes multiple arguments into a sequence of functions that each take a single argument. f(a, b, c) becomes f(a)(b)(c).
analogy: Like a coffee order that gets more specific with each step: first you choose size, then type, then additions. Each choice returns a more specific order function.
tiny_visual_key: one box splitting into chain of single-input boxes
example: const add = a => b => c => a + b + c; add(1)(2)(3) returns 6. Each call returns a new function until all arguments are provided.
why_it_matters: Currying enables partial application, point-free style, and building specialized functions from general ones. It's fundamental to composition.
checkpoint_question: What's the benefit of currying a function like add(a, b)?
expected_answer: You can create specialized versions like add5 = add(5), then use add5(3) to get 8. It lets you configure functions incrementally and reuse partial configurations.
common_mistake: Confusing currying (transforming arity) with partial application (fixing some arguments). Currying enables partial application but they're different concepts.
key_insight: Currying turns any function into a pipeline of single-argument functions, making composition and specialization natural.

title: Function Composition
explanation: Function composition combines two or more functions to create a new function. The output of one function becomes the input of the next: compose(f, g)(x) = f(g(x)).
analogy: Like an assembly line where each station does one thing. The product moves through stations in order: raw material -> cut -> paint -> package.
tiny_visual_key: chain of function boxes with arrows flowing through
example: const compose = (f, g) => x => f(g(x)); const addOne = x => x + 1; const double = x => x * 2; compose(double, addOne)(5) = 12
why_it_matters: Composition builds complex transformations from simple functions. It encourages small, focused functions that combine flexibly.
checkpoint_question: In compose(f, g)(x), which function executes first?
expected_answer: g executes first with x, then f executes with g's result. Composition reads right-to-left (or inner-to-outer), like mathematical notation.
common_mistake: Getting the order wrong. compose applies functions right-to-left. Use pipe for left-to-right if that's more intuitive.
key_insight: Composition is the fundamental way to build programs in FP - combine small pure functions into larger ones without intermediate variables.

title: Partial Application
explanation: Partial application creates a new function by fixing some arguments of an existing function. The new function takes the remaining arguments.
analogy: Like pre-filling parts of a form. A tax form pre-filled with your address becomes a simpler form - you just need to fill in the remaining fields.
tiny_visual_key: function with some slots filled, some empty
example: const greet = (greeting, name) => greeting + ', ' + name; const sayHello = greet.bind(null, 'Hello'); sayHello('World') = 'Hello, World'
why_it_matters: Partial application creates specialized functions from general ones, reduces repetition, and makes code more expressive by encoding common configurations.
checkpoint_question: How is partial application different from simply calling a function with fewer arguments?
expected_answer: Partial application returns a new function that remembers the fixed arguments and waits for the rest. Simply calling with fewer args might error or return undefined.
common_mistake: Using currying when partial application would be clearer. Currying is a transformation; partial application is about fixing specific arguments.
key_insight: Partial application lets you create a family of related functions from one general function by progressively fixing parameters.

title: Map
explanation: Map applies a transformation function to each element of a collection, returning a new collection of the same size with transformed elements.
analogy: Like a photo filter applied to every photo in an album. Each photo is transformed the same way, and you get a new album with all filtered photos.
tiny_visual_key: row of boxes with arrows each going through same transform to new row
example: [1, 2, 3].map(x => x * 2) returns [2, 4, 6]. Each element is doubled independently.
why_it_matters: Map is the fundamental transformation operation. It lets you describe what to do to each element without writing loop boilerplate.
checkpoint_question: Why does map always return an array of the same length as the input?
expected_answer: Because map applies the function to each element exactly once and collects all results. It's a one-to-one transformation - every input produces exactly one output.
common_mistake: Using map when you don't need the result array. If you're just doing side effects, use forEach. Map is for transformations.
key_insight: Map preserves structure while changing contents. The shape of your data stays the same; only the values change.

title: Filter
explanation: Filter tests each element against a predicate function and returns a new collection containing only elements that pass the test.
analogy: Like a bouncer at a club checking IDs. Everyone approaches, but only those meeting the criteria get through. The bouncer doesn't change anyone, just decides who enters.
tiny_visual_key: row of boxes going through gate, some pass through, some blocked
example: [1, 2, 3, 4, 5].filter(x => x % 2 === 0) returns [2, 4]. Only even numbers pass the test.
why_it_matters: Filter lets you select a subset of data declaratively. Combined with map, you can select and transform in expressive pipelines.
checkpoint_question: Why might filter return an empty array?
expected_answer: If no elements pass the predicate test, filter returns an empty array. This is normal - it means nothing matched the criteria.
common_mistake: Trying to use filter to transform elements. Filter only selects - use map for transformation, or use reduce for both.
key_insight: Filter changes the quantity of elements but not their values. It's about selection, not transformation.

title: Reduce (Fold)
explanation: Reduce processes a collection element by element, accumulating a single result. Each step combines the current accumulator with the next element using a reducer function.
analogy: Like making a snowball by rolling it through snow. You start with a small ball (initial value), and each roll (element) makes it bigger (accumulates). You end with one big snowball.
tiny_visual_key: row of boxes feeding into single growing accumulator box
example: [1, 2, 3, 4].reduce((sum, n) => sum + n, 0) returns 10. Starting from 0, each number is added to the accumulator.
why_it_matters: Reduce is the most powerful array method - map and filter can be implemented using reduce. It can transform arrays into any shape: objects, numbers, other arrays.
checkpoint_question: What happens if you don't provide an initial value to reduce?
expected_answer: The first element becomes the initial accumulator and iteration starts from the second element. This fails on empty arrays and can cause type issues.
common_mistake: Forgetting to return the accumulator. Each iteration must return the new accumulator value, or you'll get undefined.
key_insight: Reduce is about aggregation - taking many values and combining them into one (of any type). It's the fundamental fold operation.

title: FlatMap
explanation: FlatMap (or chain/bind) applies a function that returns a collection to each element, then flattens the results into a single collection.
analogy: Like asking each person in a group to list their friends. You get multiple lists, then combine them into one big list of all friends.
tiny_visual_key: boxes each exploding into multiple boxes, then merging into one row
why_it_matters: FlatMap handles operations that expand into multiple results. It's essential for chaining operations that might produce zero, one, or many results per input.
checkpoint_question: How is flatMap different from map followed by flat?
expected_answer: Functionally they're the same: flatMap(fn) equals map(fn).flat(1). But flatMap is more efficient (one pass) and expresses the intent more clearly.
common_mistake: Using map when you need flatMap. If your map produces nested arrays you'll have to flatten, flatMap is the right choice.
key_insight: FlatMap is the monadic bind operation - it allows sequencing operations that produce wrapped values without accumulating layers of wrapping.

title: Recursion Basics
explanation: Recursion is when a function calls itself to solve a problem by breaking it into smaller instances of the same problem. It needs a base case to stop and a recursive case to continue.
analogy: Like Russian nesting dolls. To find what's inside, you open a doll and find a smaller doll. Keep opening until you reach the smallest solid doll (base case).
tiny_visual_key: function box with arrow looping back, getting smaller each time
example: factorial(n): if n <= 1 return 1, else return n * factorial(n-1). factorial(3) = 3 * 2 * 1 = 6
why_it_matters: Recursion naturally expresses self-similar problems like tree traversal, divide-and-conquer algorithms, and mathematical definitions. It replaces loops in functional programming.
checkpoint_question: What happens if a recursive function has no base case?
expected_answer: It causes infinite recursion - the function keeps calling itself forever until the call stack overflows and the program crashes with a stack overflow error.
common_mistake: Making the recursive call with the same arguments, leading to infinite recursion. Each call must progress toward the base case.
key_insight: Think recursively by assuming the recursive call works for smaller inputs, then figure out how to use that result for the current input.

title: Tail Recursion
explanation: A tail recursive function has its recursive call as the very last operation. The result of the recursive call is directly returned without any additional computation.
analogy: Like giving someone else complete instructions to finish a task rather than waiting for them to report back. You're done, they take over completely.
tiny_visual_key: chain of function calls that don't need to return
example: Non-tail: return n * factorial(n-1) - must wait for result to multiply. Tail: return factorial(n-1, n*acc) - result is directly returned.
why_it_matters: Tail recursive functions can be optimized by the compiler to use constant stack space (tail call optimization), preventing stack overflow for deep recursion.
checkpoint_question: Why can't 'return n * factorial(n-1)' be tail-call optimized?
expected_answer: Because after factorial(n-1) returns, there's still work to do - multiplying by n. The stack frame must be kept to remember n for the multiplication.
common_mistake: Assuming all recursive calls in tail position will be optimized. Not all languages/runtimes support TCO (JavaScript engines vary).
key_insight: Convert to tail recursion by moving computation into an accumulator parameter, so the recursive call has nothing left to do.

title: Option/Maybe Type
explanation: Option (or Maybe) is a type that represents a value that might not exist. It's either Some(value) or None, forcing explicit handling of the absence case.
analogy: Like a gift box that might be empty. Instead of just handing someone something that might be nothing, you hand them a box they must open and check.
tiny_visual_key: box labeled Some containing value, or empty box labeled None
example: findUser(id) returns Option<User>. You must pattern match or map over it - you can't accidentally use a missing user.
why_it_matters: Option eliminates null pointer exceptions by making absence explicit in the type system. The compiler ensures you handle both cases.
checkpoint_question: How is Option better than returning null for missing values?
expected_answer: Option forces you to handle the missing case at compile time - you can't accidentally call methods on a None. Null can be forgotten and cause runtime crashes.
common_mistake: Immediately unwrapping Option with get() or equivalent. This defeats the purpose. Use map, flatMap, or getOrElse instead.
key_insight: Option makes null-safety a first-class concern. Instead of hoping values exist, you declare uncertainty in types.

title: Either/Result Type
explanation: Either represents a value that can be one of two types: typically Right for success or Left for error. Unlike Option, Either carries error information.
analogy: Like a letter that's either an acceptance (Right/success with details) or rejection (Left/error with reason). Both carry information, not just success/failure.
tiny_visual_key: fork showing Left path with error, Right path with value
example: divide(a, b) returns Either<Error, number>. Right(5) for success, Left('Division by zero') for failure.
why_it_matters: Either makes error handling explicit and composable. Errors flow through computations automatically without try/catch, and you can chain happy-path operations.
checkpoint_question: Why use Either instead of throwing exceptions?
expected_answer: Either makes errors part of the return type - visible and mandatory to handle. Exceptions are invisible in function signatures and can be forgotten, causing runtime crashes.
common_mistake: Using Either for truly exceptional cases that can't be handled. Either is for expected failure cases like validation errors, not for bugs.
key_insight: Either enables railway-oriented programming - success cases flow right, errors short-circuit left, and you handle both at the end.

title: Sum Types (Tagged Unions)
explanation: A sum type is a type that can be one of several variants, each potentially holding different data. Also called tagged unions or discriminated unions.
analogy: Like a shipping label that says 'This is a BOOK' or 'This is FRAGILE_ELECTRONICS'. The label tells you which type it is and how to handle it.
tiny_visual_key: multiple labeled variants pointing to one type
example: type Shape = Circle(radius) | Rectangle(w, h) | Triangle(a, b, c). A Shape is exactly one of these.
why_it_matters: Sum types model domain concepts that have distinct variants. Pattern matching ensures you handle all cases, catching missing logic at compile time.
checkpoint_question: How do sum types prevent handling only some cases?
expected_answer: The compiler can check pattern matches for exhaustiveness. If you add a new variant, all matches must be updated or you get a compile error.
common_mistake: Using class hierarchies when sum types are simpler. For a fixed set of variants with different data, sum types are clearer.
key_insight: Sum types + pattern matching = the compiler verifies you handle all cases. This catches bugs that class hierarchies miss.

title: Product Types
explanation: A product type combines multiple types together - like a struct or tuple. The values of a product type contain a value from each component type.
analogy: Like a meal combo containing a burger AND fries AND drink. You get all three - they're bundled together.
tiny_visual_key: multiple boxes combined into one box with AND
example: type Person = (name: String, age: Int, email: String) - a Person has all three fields.
why_it_matters: Product types let you bundle related data together with compile-time guarantees that all fields are present and correctly typed.
checkpoint_question: Why are they called 'product' types?
expected_answer: Because the number of possible values is the product of each component's possibilities. If name has N values and age has M values, Person has N * M possible values.
common_mistake: Using product types when sum types are more accurate. If something is A or B (not both), use a sum type.
key_insight: Sum types are OR (one of many), product types are AND (all of several). Most real data combines both.

title: Functors
explanation: A functor is a type that can be mapped over. It wraps a value and provides a map function that applies a function to the wrapped value while preserving the structure.
analogy: Like a wrapped gift. You can transform what's inside (map over it) without unwrapping - the box shape stays the same, only contents change.
tiny_visual_key: container box with map arrow transforming contents inside
example: Array is a functor - map transforms contents while keeping array structure. Option is a functor - map transforms the value if present.
why_it_matters: Functors provide a uniform interface for applying transformations to wrapped values. Code written against the functor interface works with any functor.
checkpoint_question: What must be true for map to be a valid functor implementation?
expected_answer: Two laws: identity (mapping identity function returns the same functor) and composition (mapping f then g equals mapping f composed with g).
common_mistake: Thinking functor is the same as 'can loop over'. Functor is about structure-preserving transformation, not iteration.
key_insight: Functors abstract over 'things that can be mapped'. Once you see the pattern, you recognize it everywhere: arrays, optionals, promises, trees.

title: Monads
explanation: A monad is a type that wraps values and provides flatMap (bind/chain) for sequencing operations that also return wrapped values, plus a way to wrap values (unit/return).
analogy: Like a production line where each station produces a box. Without monad, boxes would nest inside boxes. FlatMap opens each box before passing to the next station.
tiny_visual_key: chain of boxes being opened and repacked at each step
example: Promise is a monad: .then is flatMap. Instead of Promise<Promise<value>>, you get Promise<value>. Operations chain cleanly.
why_it_matters: Monads solve the nested wrapper problem. They let you chain operations that each add a layer of context (async, nullable, error) without accumulating layers.
checkpoint_question: Why do we need flatMap instead of just map for chaining operations?
expected_answer: If each operation returns a wrapped value and you use map, you get nested wrappers (Promise<Promise<x>>). FlatMap flattens one layer, keeping the chain flat.
common_mistake: Getting lost in abstract definitions. Think practically: monad = chainable wrapper with a flatten operation built in.
key_insight: Monads are about sequencing effects. The effect could be anything: async, errors, state, IO. FlatMap sequences while handling the effect.

title: Type Classes
explanation: Type classes define behavior that types can implement. They're like interfaces but can be added to existing types without modifying them, and can provide default implementations.
analogy: Like a certification that any person can earn. You don't have to be born with it - anyone can learn the skills. And the certification can be added after the person exists.
tiny_visual_key: badge being attached to different type boxes
example: Eq type class defines equality. Any type with an equals implementation can be Eq. You can make your custom type Eq without changing the type class.
why_it_matters: Type classes enable ad-hoc polymorphism - generic functions that work on any type with the right capabilities, decided at compile time.
checkpoint_question: How are type classes different from interfaces/traits?
expected_answer: Type classes can be added to types after they're defined (retroactive conformance), can have default implementations, and select implementation at compile time based on type.
common_mistake: Thinking type classes and interfaces are the same. The key difference is retroactive conformance - adding capabilities to existing types.
key_insight: Type classes separate the 'what' (interface) from 'how' (implementation) and 'who' (which type), allowing maximum flexibility.

title: Lazy Evaluation
explanation: Lazy evaluation delays computation until the result is actually needed. Values are only computed when first accessed, and results can be cached for reuse.
analogy: Like a recipe you only cook when someone orders the dish. You don't make all dishes in advance - you wait for demand, then cook and serve.
tiny_visual_key: sleeping computation box with 'wake on access' label
example: In Haskell, [1..] is an infinite list that doesn't crash because values are only computed when accessed. take 5 [1..] gives [1,2,3,4,5].
why_it_matters: Laziness enables infinite data structures, avoids unnecessary computation, and allows separation of data generation from data consumption.
checkpoint_question: How does lazy evaluation enable infinite data structures?
expected_answer: Values are only computed when accessed. An infinite list doesn't compute all elements - just those you ask for. The 'infinite' part is never actually evaluated.
common_mistake: Assuming lazy evaluation is always better. Laziness adds overhead for thunk management and can cause space leaks if not careful.
key_insight: Laziness decouples 'what' from 'when'. You define what to compute, and the runtime decides when (if ever) to actually do it.

title: Infinite Data Structures
explanation: With lazy evaluation, you can define data structures of infinite size. Only the portion you access is actually computed, so infinity is just a potential, never a reality.
analogy: Like a magic scroll that keeps unrolling as you read. You can never reach the end, but you also never need to hold the whole scroll at once.
tiny_visual_key: scroll with visible portion and arrows indicating endless continuation
example: The infinite list of Fibonacci numbers: [1, 1, 2, 3, 5, ...]. You can take the first 100 without generating all of them.
why_it_matters: Infinite structures let you separate 'all possible values' from 'values I need right now'. This simplifies code by removing manual stopping conditions.
checkpoint_question: What determines how much of an infinite structure is actually computed?
expected_answer: Consumer demand. Only the elements you actually access are computed. Functions like 'take', 'filter', or indexing drive computation.
common_mistake: Trying to force/evaluate an entire infinite structure (printing it, finding its length, etc.). This never terminates.
key_insight: Infinite data structures shift control from producer to consumer. The consumer decides how much to compute.

title: Point-Free Style
explanation: Point-free (or tacit) programming writes functions without explicitly mentioning their arguments. Functions are defined as compositions of other functions.
analogy: Like saying 'Apply double, then add one' instead of 'Take x, double x, then add one to the result'. The data flows implicitly through the pipeline.
tiny_visual_key: pipeline of function names with no variable boxes
example: Instead of x => f(g(x)), write compose(f, g). Instead of x => x.length, write prop('length').
why_it_matters: Point-free style emphasizes data flow and transformation pipelines. It can make composition clearer by focusing on operations rather than data plumbing.
checkpoint_question: When should you NOT use point-free style?
expected_answer: When it makes code harder to read - complex compositions, multiple uses of the same argument, or when variable names add clarity. Readability comes first.
common_mistake: Forcing point-free everywhere. If it requires obscure combinators or makes code confusing, just use explicit arguments.
key_insight: Point-free highlights what transformations are applied, not what data flows through. Use it when it clarifies, not as a goal in itself.

title: Lenses
explanation: Lenses provide a composable way to access and update nested immutable data structures. They combine a getter and a setter into a reusable, composable unit.
analogy: Like a precision tool that can reach deep into a nested structure, grab exactly what you need, or carefully replace a part - all without disturbing anything else.
tiny_visual_key: magnifying glass zooming into nested boxes with get/set arrows
example: A lens for user.address.city lets you get or set the city without manually copying the entire user and address objects.
why_it_matters: Lenses solve the deeply nested update problem in immutable data. Instead of manual spreading at each level, compose lenses and apply the change at the end.
checkpoint_question: Why do we need lenses for immutable data but not mutable?
expected_answer: With mutable data, you just modify in place: user.address.city = 'NYC'. With immutable data, you must copy every level. Lenses automate that copying.
common_mistake: Building lens libraries from scratch. Use established libraries (Ramda, monocle, optics-ts) that handle edge cases.
key_insight: Lenses decompose data access into composable pieces. Compose lenses to zoom deeper, apply them to get or set at any depth.

title: Transducers
explanation: Transducers are composable transformation pipelines that work on any data source. They separate the transformation logic from how data is processed and collected.
analogy: Like reusable assembly line instructions. The same instructions work whether items come on a conveyor belt, in boxes, or one at a time.
tiny_visual_key: transformation steps detached from data source and destination
example: A filter-then-map transducer works on arrays, streams, or observables without modification. The transformation is decoupled from the data structure.
why_it_matters: Transducers enable efficient processing (single pass, no intermediate collections) and work across different data types. They're especially useful for large or streaming data.
checkpoint_question: How do transducers avoid creating intermediate arrays in a map-filter-map pipeline?
expected_answer: Transducers compose the transformations into a single function applied to each element. Instead of building an array after each step, one transformed result feeds directly into the next transformation.
common_mistake: Overcomplicating simple cases. For small arrays, regular map/filter is clearer. Transducers shine for performance-critical or streaming scenarios.
key_insight: Transducers separate 'what transformation' from 'what data structure'. Compose transformations once, apply them to any iterable.

title: Managing Side Effects
explanation: Functional programs isolate side effects (IO, mutations, randomness) from pure computation. Effects are described as values, then executed at the program boundary.
analogy: Like a chef writing a recipe (description) vs actually cooking (execution). Keep the recipe pure and testable; cooking happens once at mealtime.
tiny_visual_key: pure function core with effects pushed to outer shell
example: Instead of calling fetch() directly, return an object describing the fetch. A runner at the edge of your program executes all effect descriptions.
why_it_matters: Separating description from execution makes code testable (inject mock effects), composable (combine descriptions freely), and easier to reason about.
checkpoint_question: How does describing effects as data help with testing?
expected_answer: You can inspect the effect descriptions without executing them. Tests verify correct descriptions are produced, then either mock the execution or skip it entirely.
common_mistake: Taking 'no side effects' too literally. The goal is to push effects to the boundary, not eliminate them - programs must interact with the world.
key_insight: Effects as values: describe what to do, don't do it. This keeps core logic pure and testable while still doing real work at the boundaries.

title: IO Monad
explanation: The IO monad wraps computations that interact with the outside world. It doesn't execute the effect - it represents it as a value that can be combined with other IO actions.
analogy: Like a detailed script for a movie scene. The script describes exactly what happens, but nothing actually happens until 'Action!' is called on set.
tiny_visual_key: lazy effect wrapped in IO box, awaiting trigger
example: IO(() => console.log('Hi')) doesn't log anything. It creates a description of logging. Only when you 'run' the IO does the log happen.
why_it_matters: IO makes effects explicit in the type system. Pure functions return pure values; impure functions return IO. The type tells you what a function does.
checkpoint_question: How does IO maintain purity while allowing side effects?
expected_answer: IO wraps effects in a lazy thunk. Creating an IO value is pure - it just stores a function. The impure part (running the function) happens only once at the program's edge.
common_mistake: Unwrapping IO deep in the code (calling run or unsafePerformIO). Keep IO wrapped and compose it - only run at the very top of your program.
key_insight: IO isn't about preventing effects - it's about making them visible. An IO type signature says 'this does something to the world.'

title: Functional Error Handling
explanation: Functional error handling uses types like Either and Result instead of exceptions. Errors become values that flow through computations and must be explicitly handled.
analogy: Like a form that returns to you marked 'valid' with data or 'invalid' with the reason. You must check which it is before proceeding - no silent failures.
tiny_visual_key: result branching to success or error path, both explicit
example: parseJSON(str) returns Either<ParseError, Object>. You can chain operations with map/flatMap; errors short-circuit automatically.
why_it_matters: Type-based errors make failure explicit, composable, and impossible to forget. No more uncaught exceptions or crashed programs from unhandled errors.
checkpoint_question: How does Either make error handling more composable than try/catch?
expected_answer: Either values can be mapped and chained like success values. Errors automatically propagate through the chain. Try/catch forces you to handle errors at each call site.
common_mistake: Converting Either to exceptions at boundaries. Let Either flow through your code - only handle at the end or when you actually need to branch.
key_insight: Make errors values, not control flow. Values can be transformed, combined, and inspected. Thrown exceptions just disappear upward.

title: Functional Programming in Practice
explanation: Pragmatic FP takes useful concepts (immutability, pure functions, composition) without requiring full monad stacks. Modern languages blend FP and OOP features.
analogy: Like using ergonomic tools from a specialized toolkit. You don't need to become a master carpenter to benefit from a well-designed hammer.
tiny_visual_key: toolbox with selected FP tools, not everything used
example: Use map/filter/reduce, keep functions pure where possible, use immutable updates, compose small functions - without requiring Haskell.
why_it_matters: You don't need a purely functional language to benefit from FP. React, Redux, RxJS all use functional concepts in mainstream JavaScript.
checkpoint_question: What FP concepts provide the most benefit in everyday code?
expected_answer: Pure functions (predictable, testable), immutability (no surprise mutations), higher-order functions (reusable transformations), and composition (building complex from simple).
common_mistake: Going all-in on FP theory before mastering basics. Start with pure functions and immutability - they provide most of the benefit.
key_insight: The best FP is invisible - code that's naturally simple, predictable, and composable. You're doing FP when you're not fighting your code.
